The morning fog rolled across the river like something alive, erasing the far bank first, then the middle, then the world. I sat on the dock, watching the water turn silver, wondering if I was remembering the town or inventing it. The air smelled of wet wood and old rain, and the birds moved through the gray air with the quiet confidence of things that had always known the answer.

My father would have stopped here. He liked the place where the water became still enough to show you your own face without flinching. He was gone now, and I kept finding him in small things: the creak of the dock, the way the light touched the railing, the particular silence after a car passes too quickly. Memory, I had learned, does not behave like a photograph. It breathes. It changes. It leaves out the bad parts so you can keep living.

Below, a fish broke the surface, then vanished, and the water smoothed itself over the wound. I thought about how easily that could have been the point of the whole morning: not to fix anything, not to become someone else, only to watch something survive a small disturbance.

The fog thinned. The bank returned, tree by tree. I put my hands in my pockets, felt the cold bite my skin, and decided to walk. Not anywhere in particular. Just forward, into the day that had already begun without asking permission. The fog was not ending, but beginning again.
